valdex.tagline: Ground stations and flight hardware for the rocketry community.
valdex.overview: Valdex LLC is my engineering company. Our flagship is VX Telemetry, a ground station that runs on macOS, Windows, and Linux and works with almost any flight computer. Next up is the VX hardware line: a flight computer, a ground receiver, and a pyro deck, designed so every sensor maps straight into the software.
valdex.detail1: Shipped. Live mission control, a 3D vehicle that flies from your data, and a simulator so you can rehearse before launch day.
valdex.detail2: Three reference boards in development: Board A flight computer, Board B USB LoRa ground receiver, and Board C eight-channel pyro deck.
valdex.detail3: Mission-control software built for specific vehicles, like the ground station for KnightsRP's Phantom Boom Prize jet.

restem.overview: ReSTEM is the nonprofit I founded. More on what we're building soon.

sunflower.tagline: It lands, finds the sun, and opens up. Flown at IREC 2026.
sunflower.overview: Sunflower is the payload my SHPE UCF team built and flew aboard Odysseus at IREC 2026. The idea is in the name: after landing, it orients itself and raises a solar panel on a scissor lift, like a flower turning toward the sun. Then we open-sourced everything, every CAD file, the bill of materials, and the flight code, so anyone can build one.
sunflower.detail1: A motor-driven planetary gear system rotates the payload so the panel can face the right way, with a BNO085 9-axis IMU telling it which way is up.
sunflower.detail2: Stepper-driven lead screws raise the solar panel on a scissor mechanism. An elevator and retention system integrate the whole payload into Odysseus's nose section.
sunflower.detail3: ESP32 running ESP-IDF on FreeRTOS with a flight state machine. IMU runs at high priority, tracking at medium, and logging to SD at low, so sensor data is never dropped. Power comes from a LiFePO4 pack.

odysseus.tagline: UCF at Spaceport America. Flown, recovered, and carrying our payload.
odysseus.overview: Odysseus is the rocket UCF flew at IREC 2026 at Spaceport America as Team 25. It carried our Sunflower payload in the nose and came home in one piece. I was there for all of it: the expo floor, the rail, liftoff, and the walk out to recover it.
odysseus.detail1: The model above is the real flight assembly: 347 bodies, from the nose cone and payload bay down to the fin can. Hit Explore and pull it apart.
odysseus.detail2: Sunflower rides in the nose section on its own retention and elevator hardware, so the payload and the rocket were designed together, not bolted together at the end.
odysseus.detail3: Redundant commercial altimeters, including a PerfectFlite StratoLogger CF, mounted on a 3D-printed avionics sled and bench-tested before the trip.

monkeybar.tagline: Launch it. Land it. Aim it. A two-stage guided rocket.
monkeybar.overview: Monkey Bar is my most ambitious build: launch a rocket, land it, and aim it. The booster carries two thrust vector control mounts to come back down under control. The upper stage, Dart, uses canards to steer onto a ground target, and we score it on accuracy, not speed. A Yagi-linked ground station and a dedicated launch system tie it together.
monkeybar.detail1: Two stages. The booster lands itself on dual TVC mounts. Dart steers onto a target with canard fins.
monkeybar.detail2: Live onboard data over a Yagi antenna link, so we can make safety calls in real time, every phase of flight.
monkeybar.detail3: Reliable launches, a clean landing zone for the booster, and a safe range to measure exactly where Dart lands.

phantom.tagline: The mission-control app for our Mach 1 attempt.
phantom.overview: When you're trying to push an RC jet past Mach 1, you can't afford to guess what the engine is doing. I built Phantom's ground station as a native desktop app that reads our LoRa link over USB serial, or runs the full mission profile in simulation, behind one interface. The dashboard, alerts, and abort logic behave the same either way, so rehearsal is real practice.
phantom.detail1: Mach is the biggest thing on the screen, because it's the only number that wins. Around it: airspeed, altitude, attitude, dynamic pressure with a redline, GPS ground track, G-load, CG, and full turbine health: RPM, EGT, fuel flow, and time-to-empty.
phantom.detail2: An armed or abort kill-switch indicator you can't miss, a fault-injection menu to rehearse engine and link failures, checklists, and a source chip that makes it impossible to mistake a simulation for a real flight.
phantom.detail3: A versioned key=value serial format with CRC-16 checks and a reference encoder our firmware team builds against. I can test the whole radio path end to end before the hardware even exists.

vxtelemetry.tagline: Plug in any flight computer. Watch your flight live.
vxtelemetry.overview: Most teams I've seen at launches have the same problem: great avionics, and a ground station held together with a script someone wrote the night before. So I built the one I wanted. VX Telemetry recognizes your data stream and puts it on a real mission-control dashboard. No parsing code. It runs on macOS, Windows, and Linux, and it's built for everything from a first L1 flight to IREC and NASA Student Launch.
vxtelemetry.detail1: A mission clock, a flight-phase track from pad to landing, a GO/NO-GO board, drag-aware apogee prediction on the way up, and touchdown ETA on the way down. Liftoff is accelerometer-gated and apogee is a debounced fused-velocity zero crossing, so one bad baro reading never calls a false apogee.
vxtelemetry.detail2: Drop in your own CAD and watch it fly from real telemetry attitude, with staging, drogue, and main deploys animated off the actual flight events. A baro and accelerometer Kalman filter gives you smoothed altitude and the velocity most flight computers never transmit.
vxtelemetry.detail3: An NDJSON frame contract with automatic aliases, plus CSV and key=value ingest, so most altimeters and flight computers just work. Anything that doesn't, you map in the app. Optional CRC-16 on the wire and packet counters give you true link-loss numbers.

harper.tagline: The road to Level 1. Two attempts, one rocket philosophy.
harper.overview: Harper is my Level 1 high-power certification rocket. The first attempt, flown on an H169, did not earn the certification. Every lesson from that flight is going into attempt two.
harper.detail1: My first Level 1 design and first certification flight, on an H169. It didn't certify. That flight taught me more than a clean one would have.
harper.detail2: Attempt two is a revised Harper built on everything the first flight showed me. I'll post the new model and the result here.
harper.detail3: Certification is how you earn the right to fly bigger motors. Getting there the hard way is part of the story.

charlotte.tagline: The next altitude. Built for Level 2.
charlotte.overview: Charlotte is my Level 2 high-power rocket, now on its fifth design revision and working toward certification on J, K, and L class motors.
charlotte.detail1: Charlotte is on V5. Each revision tightened the design before I commit to a Level 2 flight.
charlotte.detail2: L2 opens up J, K, and L motors, which means more energy, more speed, and less margin for a sloppy airframe.
charlotte.detail3: Finish Level 1 with Harper, then fly Charlotte for L2.

phantomjet.tagline: Mach 1. Twice. Same day. No rockets allowed.
phantomjet.overview: Boom Supersonic put up $800,000 for the first amateur RC aircraft to break the sound barrier, and I want it. Phantom is KnightsRP's answer: a slender, turbine-powered delta built to do something no hobbyist has ever done. I'm designing the airframe structure and propulsion assembly, and I already wrote the mission-control software we'll fly it with.
phantomjet.detail1: Exceed the local speed of sound in level or climbing flight, no diving, and hold it for at least five seconds after accelerating from Mach 0.8. Then land, take off, and do it again the other direction the same day, in front of judges including NASA's Jared Isaacman and SpaceX's Tom Mueller. Max takeoff weight is 25 kg, and it has to be a turbojet, turbofan, or ramjet. Rockets are banned.
phantomjet.detail2: A long, slender fuselage with an ogive-delta wing, shaped to slip through the transonic drag rise instead of fighting it. Inside, it's a frame of ring bulkheads and longerons carrying the loads to the wing, with the turbine housed in its own aft propulsion section. Every gram matters when you're chasing Mach 1 under 25 kg.
phantomjet.detail3: I didn't want to fly a supersonic attempt blind, so I built the ground station first. It puts Mach front and center, watches EGT, RPM, fuel, and dynamic pressure against redlines, and runs the planned profile in simulation: climb, accelerate through Mach 0.95 to 1.10, decelerate, land.

about.intro: I'm an aerospace engineering student at UCF. I learn by building: flight hardware, ground stations, and the software in between. I founded Valdex LLC and the ReSTEM nonprofit, and I'm chasing the Boom Prize with KnightsRP.

experience.text: Designing the airframe structure and propulsion assembly for a supersonic RC jet, and building its mission-control ground station.
Built and flew a self-orienting solar payload aboard Odysseus at Spaceport America. Fully open source.
Flew with Team 25 at the Intercollegiate Rocket Engineering Competition.
Shipped VX Telemetry, a cross-platform rocketry ground station. Building the VX hardware line.
Working through Level 1 and Level 2 high-power certification.
